name: Learn a new programming language
description: Pick up a new language by building real things: syntax, standard library, tooling, testing and a complete final project. Works for any language, from Rust to Python to Kotlin.

steps.title: Set up the toolchain
steps.description: Install the compiler or runtime, an editor with language support, a formatter, a linter and the package manager. Run a Hello world and a first test.

steps.title: Syntax tour: variables, types and control flow
steps.description: Work through the official tutorial. Re-type every example instead of pasting it and change it to see what breaks.

steps.title: Functions, modules and error handling
steps.description: Learn how code is split into files and packages, and how this language reports and handles errors.

steps.title: Data structures and the standard library
steps.description: Lists, maps, sets, strings, dates, files and JSON. Learn what the standard library already gives you before reaching for a package.

steps.title: Type system and object model
steps.description: Classes, interfaces, traits, generics or whatever this language uses to model things, and how it differs from the languages you know.

steps.title: Idioms and style
steps.description: Read the official style guide and the code of a well-respected project. Note what experienced developers do differently from a beginner.

steps.title: Testing and debugging
steps.description: Write unit tests for your katas, learn the debugger and the profiler, and measure coverage.

steps.title: Concurrency or asynchronous code
steps.description: Understand the model this language uses (threads, async/await, goroutines, actors) and the classic pitfalls.

steps.title: Practice katas: solve familiar problems again
steps.description: Re-solve about fifteen problems you already know how to solve in another language. Compare with idiomatic solutions afterwards.

steps.title: Final project: small but complete
steps.description: Plan, build, test and document a real tool or application. Publish it or demo it to someone.

steps.title: Read a popular library and review your project
steps.description: Read the source of one widely used library and refactor your project with what you learned.

competencies.name: Syntax and types
competencies.description: Write correct code in the language without looking up the basics.

competencies.name: Standard library
competencies.description: Know what the standard library offers and use it before adding dependencies.

competencies.name: Tooling and testing
competencies.description: Build, test, debug, format and package projects with the language's tools.

competencies.name: Idiomatic style
competencies.description: Write code that other developers of this language find natural to read.

competencies.name: Building projects
competencies.description: Design and finish a complete program, not only exercises.

routines.title: Read code from a good project

cards.back: A function bundled with the variables of the scope where it was created, so it can keep using them even when called elsewhere.
The stack holds call frames and local values, allocated and freed automatically in order. The heap holds objects that live as long as something refers to them or until they are freed.
It cannot change under your feet: easier to reason about, safe to share between threads and simple to test.

cards.front: What does every recursive function need?
cards.back: A base case that stops the recursion, and a step that moves each call closer to that base case.
O(log n), on sorted data: each comparison halves the remaining search space.
A function whose result depends only on its arguments and which has no side effects. The same input always gives the same output.
One that can be repeated with the same effect as doing it once, for example setting a value, as opposed to incrementing it.
A bug where the result depends on the unpredictable timing of two or more threads or tasks accessing shared state.
Compiled code is translated to machine code or bytecode before running; interpreted code is executed by another program line by line. Many languages mix both.
With value semantics, assignment copies the data. With reference semantics, assignment copies a pointer, so both names see the same object.
